_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 9 Light and Seeing. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the five parts of LESSON[lecture] in content/lesson-9.py in order (straight lines; reflection; seeing; the old idea; and today's ray diagram), with the lesson's mirror experiment as its own chapter between reflection and seeing, where the lesson puts it. The pictures are the lesson's own where it has one: its mirror experiment (ART.sim rayMirror, the three states its two buttons reach) and its labelling figure (ART.figure ray, with the four parts its diagram step asks the child to name). Every ray in this film travels source to object to eye; the one place a ray leaves an eye is the old idea in the How the idea changed chapter, which is crossed out as the line says it was wrong.
title: Light and Seeing
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Know that light travels in straight lines and this can be represented with ray diagrams.
Know that light can reflect off surfaces.
Describe how objects which are not light sources are seen.
Draw a diagram to represent a real world situation and/or scientific idea.
Make a prediction describing some possible outcomes of an enquiry.
Identify whether results support, or do not support, a prediction.
Use observations and tests to sort, group and classify objects.
Describe how scientific knowledge and understanding changes over time through the use of evidence gained by enquiry.

beats.say: Light travels in straight lines. It will not bend round a corner.
You see a book when light bounces off it into your eye.
Shine a torch through dusty air. The beam is dead straight.
Sunlight through a gap in the clouds comes down in straight lines.
You cannot see round a corner. Light will not bend round it.
The light from behind the corner travels straight, and misses your eye.
Scientists draw light as rays: straight lines with arrows.
When light hits a surface, some of it bounces off. That is reflection.
A mirror reflects neatly, in one new straight line.
A book reflects roughly, scattering the light in every direction.
Pale and shiny surfaces reflect most of the light that hits them.
Dark surfaces soak most of it up, so they look dark.
A torch, a mirror and an eye. Watch what the ray does.
Predict first. Will the ray bounce, stop dead, or curve round?
Turn the mirror. It bounces off in a new straight line, as you predicted.

at.bounces: bounces off in a new straight line

beats.say: At the right angle the ray reaches the eye, and you see the torch.
Put a book in the way. It blocks the ray, so the mirror shows no torch.

at.book: Put a book in the way

beats.say: Only a light source makes light. You see everything else by reflection.

at.source: Only a light source makes light

beats.say: The lamp shines on the book. The book is not a source.

at.lamp: The lamp shines on the book

beats.say: It reflects some of that light off its surface, in every direction.
A little of it travels straight into your eye. Now you see the book.
Switch the lamp off. Nothing reflects, so you see nothing at all.
The Sun, a lamp and a candle make light. The Moon and a mirror only reflect.

at.sources: The Sun, a lamp and a candle

beats.say: For a thousand years people believed the eye sent out beams.
But if that were true, why can nobody see in a dark room?
Ibn al-Haytham built dark rooms with tiny holes and tested it.
He showed light comes into the eye, not out of it. Evidence changed what everyone knew.
Now draw it all: the light source, the ray, the mirror and the eye.
The source first. Every ray starts at the torch.
A ruler line to the mirror, with an arrow pointing away from the torch.
Then a second straight line into the eye. That is your ray diagram.
Light travels in straight lines, and we draw it as rays with arrows.
Light reflects off surfaces: neatly off a mirror, roughly off a book.
You see a thing when light from a source bounces off it into your eye.
Evidence from enquiry changed the old idea. That is how science works.
